prompt_text:
The figure summarizes the global sulfur cycle and contrasts sulfur processing in freshwater versus marine systems. At the top, a schematic cross-section of Earth shows major sulfur fluxes among the upper mantle, oceanic crust, continents, and oceans. Sulfur is exchanged through volcanism at mid-ocean ridges, subduction, and weathering on land, with rivers delivering sulfur to the ocean and crustal recycling returning it to the mantle.

The lower half compares two aquatic environments. In freshwater, sulfate availability is low, so sulfur cycling appears more tightly limited. In marine settings, high sulfate concentrations support a more extensive sulfur network. In both cases, sulfur moves between dissolved sulfate, organic sulfur compounds, plankton, bacteria, and sedimentary organic matter. Biological assimilation and remineralization connect the water column to microbes, while decomposition, hydrolysis, and reduction drive sediment processes. Reduced sulfur species such as sulfide can be reincorporated into organic matter, transformed into intermediate sulfur compounds, or ultimately locked into minerals like pyrite.

Overall, the key message is that sulfate concentration strongly shapes aquatic sulfur transformations, while these local processes are embedded within a larger tectonic and weathering-driven global sulfur cycle.
